situationBrief.title: The School Activity Logbook Mystery
situationBrief.description: Mira, Arjun, and Gyan discovered an old school activity folder with entries from yesterday, today, and tomorrow—but several verb forms are mixed up. Help repair the timeline!

beats.speaker: mira
beats.dialogue: Look at these school activity records we found! Yesterday's science club note says 'Yesterday, our team plant saplings.' That verb does not match yesterday!

beats.speaker: arjun
beats.dialogue: And look at today's note: 'Riya is knowing the answer.' Wait—can we add '-ing' to 'know', and how do we show tomorrow's plan clearly?

beats.speaker: gyan
beats.dialogue: Time is when an event happens—Past, Present, or Future. Tense is the grammatical verb form we choose to match that time and how the action unfolds. Let us travel across the timeline together!

grammarOutcomes: Distinguish real-world Time (Past, Present, Future) from verb form (Tense and Aspect).
Choose accurately between Present Simple (habits/facts) and Present Progressive (happening now), and recognise stative verbs like 'know' and 'like'.
Use Past Simple, Present Perfect, Past Progressive, and standard Future Time expressions ('will', 'going to', scheduled Present Simple).
learningObjectives.knowledgeOutcome: Explore Indian school eco-clubs, weather logs, sports practice, and ISRO astronomy club trips through accurate timelines.

sourceReferences.bookTitle: LEARN AND PRACTISE GRAMMAR CLASS - IX
sourceReferences.note: Distinguishes Time from Tense, teaches Present/Past tense forms and aspects (Simple, Progressive, Perfect, Perfect Progressive), stative non-progressive verbs (p. 43), and Future Time expressions (pp. 57-61).

sourceReferences.bookTitle: A Practice Book of ENGLISH GRAMMAR & COMPOSITION (GRAMMAR IN USE) for Class IX
sourceReferences.note: Summarises 12 traditional tense usages (Present/Past/Future x Indefinite/Continuous/Perfect/Perfect Continuous), time adverbs, and Sequence of Tenses.

sourceReferences.bookTitle: A NEW METHOD English Grammar For Class IX & X
sourceReferences.note: Distinguishes Time vs Tense (L1), presents Strong/Weak/Invariant verbs (L4), conjugation tables, stative non-continuous verbs, for/since, and common tense errors (L6).
Bridges Odisha's 2-Tense + 3-Time model with PSEB/Assam's 12-Tense naming and provides core irregular verb forms ('write/wrote/written', 'eat/ate/eaten', 'leave/left/left').

sentences.title: Present Habit Record
sentences.rawText: The sun rises in the east every morning.
sentences.note: Universal truths and daily habits stay in Present Simple regardless of 'right now'.

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Introduces the noun 'sun' inside the Subject.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names what the sentence is about (singular).
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Singular third-person Subject requiring '-s/-es' on a Present Simple verb.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Describes an action true every day.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Base verb + 's' shows Present Simple for universal facts and habits.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: Universal facts and daily routines use Present Simple, never '-ing'.

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Begins the prepositional phrase 'in the east'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the direction where the sun rises.

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Works with 'morning' as a Present Simple time clue.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Tells when the repeated action happens.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Completes the habit time clue 'every morning'.

groups.label: Subject
groups.textbookRule: Present Simple / Indefinite expresses universal truths and habitual actions (Odisha IX p. 35; PSEB IX p. 94; Assam p. 137).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.questionPrompt: What does the sun always do?
groups.plainExplanation: 'rises in the east every morning' states a permanent truth.
groups.textbookRule: The finite verb 'rises' shows Present Simple.

relationships.label: rises ← sun
relationships.explanation: 'rises' matches singular Subject 'sun' and conveys timeless Present Simple.

structureSummary.predicateText: rises in the east every morning
structureSummary.patternNote: Universal truth + 'every morning' clue → Present Simple.

sentences.title: Happening Right Now
sentences.rawText: Mira is writing the science report now.
sentences.note: Actions actively in progress at the moment of speaking take 'am/is/are + verb-ing'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the student writing right now.

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Present auxiliary 'is' combines with '-ing' participle to form Present Progressive.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Shows the action continuing at this moment.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Together, 'is writing' expresses Present Progressive / Continuous.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: Clue word 'now' shows the writing is in progress at this moment.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Signals the action is happening at this very moment.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Time clue guiding us to Present Progressive.

groups.label: Subject
groups.textbookRule: Present Progressive (am/is/are + v-ing) denotes actions going on at the time of speaking (Odisha IX p. 36; PSEB IX p. 94).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'is writing the science report now' uses Present Progressive.

relationships.label: now → is writing
relationships.explanation: 'now' anchors the verb phrase 'is writing' to the present moment.

structureSummary.predicateText: is writing the science report now

sentences.title: Stative Verb Rule
sentences.note: Verbs of knowing, feeling, and belonging usually stay in Simple form, not '-ing'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the student who holds this knowledge.
Describes a mental state, not a temporary physical motion.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: State verbs like know, understand, believe, and belong normally reject '-ing'.

groups.label: Subject
groups.textbookRule: Verbs of state/cognition (know, like, understand, belong, seem) are normally not used in Progressive form (Odisha IX p. 43; Assam pp. 139, 159).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'knows the correct answer' uses simple state form.

sentences.title: Completed Past Action
sentences.rawText: Yesterday, our eco-club planted neem saplings.
sentences.note: Finished past time markers like 'yesterday' or 'last week' pair with Past Simple (v-ed / V2).

tokens.meaningInSentence: Fixes the event in finished past time.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Past adverb telling us to use Past Simple.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Shows the eco-club belongs to our school.
Names the student group that planted saplings.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: Clue word 'Yesterday' marks a finished past event, so base 'plant' becomes 'planted'.

groups.label: Subject
groups.textbookRule: Past Simple / Indefinite denotes an action completed at a definite time in the past (Odisha IX p. 45; PSEB IX p. 95).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'Yesterday, ... planted neem saplings.' places the action in the Past.
groups.textbookRule: Definite past markers ('yesterday', 'ago', 'last week') require Past Simple.

relationships.label: Yesterday → planted
relationships.explanation: 'Yesterday' signals completed past time, requiring Past Simple 'planted'.

sentences.title: Past Action Connected to Now
sentences.rawText: Arjun has cleaned the noticeboard already.
sentences.note: Present Perfect (has/have + past participle) links a completed action to the present result.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the student who finished the task.
Connects the completed work to right now.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Combines with 'cleaned' to form Present Perfect.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Shows the noticeboard is clean right now.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: We see the clean noticeboard now; 'already' highlights completion without a specific past clock-time.
verbMeta.subjectLinkNote: Singular 'Arjun' uses 'has', whereas plural subjects use 'have'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Shows the action finished sooner than expected.

groups.label: Subject
groups.textbookRule: Present Perfect expresses an action completed in the past whose result continues into the present (Odisha IX p. 38; PSEB IX p. 94).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'has cleaned the noticeboard already' links past work to now.
groups.textbookRule: Use 'has/have + past participle' when focus is on present relevance rather than yesterday's clock time.

relationships.label: already → has cleaned
relationships.explanation: 'already' connects completed cleaning to the present moment.

sentences.title: Planned Future Time
sentences.rawText: Our class will visit the planetarium tomorrow.
sentences.note: Future time is communicated with modals ('will/shall'), 'going to', or timetable Present Simple.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names who will go on the trip.
Points the action into future time.

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: After 'will', always use the bare base verb ('visit', never 'visited').

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: Clue word 'tomorrow' refers to future time; 'will + visit' clearly expresses it.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the place we will visit.

groups.label: Subject
groups.textbookRule: Future time is shown using 'will/shall + base verb', 'be going to', Present Progressive (fixed plan), or Present Simple (timetable) (Odisha IX pp. 57-61; PSEB IX p. 96).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'will visit the planetarium tomorrow' expresses future time.
groups.textbookRule: Modal 'will' + bare infinitive 'visit' expresses future time.

relationships.label: tomorrow → will visit
relationships.explanation: 'tomorrow' signals future time, paired cleanly with 'will visit'.

teachingSequence.title: Time vs Verb Form
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: When does it happen vs how does the verb show it?
teachingSequence.explanation: Time tells us when an event happens—Past, Present, or Future. Tense is the verb form that helps communicate that time and whether the action is habitual, ongoing, or completed. Notice how 'rises' expresses a truth valid every day.

timelineData.grammarNote: Real-world Time (Past/Present/Future) and grammatical Tense work together, but they are not the same word.
timelineData.boardModelNote: Some grammar traditions describe 2 grammatical Tenses (Present & Past) plus Future Time expressions, while others list 3 Tenses (Present, Past, Future) x 4 aspects = 12 tenses. Both describe the exact same correct English sentences!

teachingSequence.title: Present Simple: Habits & Facts
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Use Present Simple for daily routines and permanent facts.
teachingSequence.explanation: When a logbook entry describes a daily habit ('every morning', 'usually', 'always') or a scientific truth ('Water boils at 100°C'), choose Present Simple—not '-ing'.

timelineData.grammarNote: Add '-s' or '-es' only when the Subject is singular third person (he, she, it, the sun).

contrastExample.incorrectText: The sun is rising in the east every morning.
contrastExample.correctText: The sun rises in the east every morning.
contrastExample.reason: 'every morning' signals a repeated habit, so Present Simple ('rises') is accurate.

teachingSequence.title: Present Progressive: Happening Now
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Use 'am / is / are + verb-ing' for actions in progress right now.
teachingSequence.explanation: Compare habits with actions happening at this very moment! Clue words like 'now', 'right now', or 'at present' show that Mira is in the middle of writing, so we use 'is writing'.

timelineData.grammarNote: Always pair the '-ing' form with an auxiliary ('am', 'is', or 'are')—never 'Mira writing now'.
timelineData.boardModelNote: Also called 'Present Continuous' in many grammar guides; both terms describe the same form (am/is/are + verb-ing).

teachingSequence.title: Stative Verbs Avoid '-ing'
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Verbs of thinking, feeling, and owning stay simple!
teachingSequence.explanation: Some verbs express a state of mind or belonging rather than a physical activity—such as 'know', 'understand', 'believe', 'like', 'own', and 'belong'. Even if true right now, say 'Riya knows', never 'is knowing'.

timelineData.grammarNote: Often called state verbs or non-conclusive verbs; they describe states of mind or feeling rather than actions in progress.

contrastExample.incorrectText: Riya is knowing the correct answer.
contrastExample.reason: 'know' describes knowledge already held, not an action in motion.

teachingSequence.title: Past Simple: Finished Past Time
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Clues like 'yesterday' and 'last week' lock in Past Simple.
teachingSequence.explanation: Look at the eco-club slip: 'Yesterday' places the action cleanly before now and finished. So base 'plant' changes to its past form 'planted' (v-ed / V2).

timelineData.grammarNote: Regular verbs add '-ed' ('planted'); irregular verbs change form ('write → wrote', 'eat → ate', 'go → went').

contrastExample.incorrectText: Yesterday, our eco-club plant neem saplings.
contrastExample.correctText: Yesterday, our eco-club planted neem saplings.
contrastExample.reason: A finished past time marker requires the Past form 'planted', not the base verb.

teachingSequence.title: Present Perfect: Linking Past to Now
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Use 'has / have + V3' when a past action matters right now.
teachingSequence.explanation: If the noticeboard is clean right now and we focus on the result ('already', 'just', 'since morning'), we use Present Perfect: 'Arjun has cleaned'. Never mix Present Perfect with 'yesterday'!

timelineData.grammarNote: Present Perfect joins past completion with a present result; never write 'has cleaned yesterday'.

teachingSequence.title: Expressing Future Time
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: English uses 'will', 'going to', and present forms for future events.
teachingSequence.explanation: For tomorrow's planetarium visit, 'will visit' clearly points ahead of now. English can also show future time with 'are going to visit', or a fixed school timetable like 'The train leaves at 6 a.m. tomorrow.'

timelineData.grammarNote: After 'will' or 'shall', always use the bare base verb ('will visit', never 'will visited').
timelineData.boardModelNote: Some grammar guides explain 'will + base verb' and 'be going to + base verb' as Future Time expressions, while others call 'will/shall + verb' Future Simple/Indefinite.

teachingSequence.title: Inspect Words Before Guided Practice
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Tap any word to see its time meaning and verb link, then start Guided Practice.
teachingSequence.explanation: Tap 'will', 'visit', or 'tomorrow' above to inspect how time clues and verb forms lock together. When you are ready, enter the Interactive Word Laboratory to sort, build, and fix logbook sentences!

wordLabActivities.title: A. Spot the Verb & Time Clue
wordLabActivities.instruction: Tap BOTH the verb phrase and the time clue word in this logbook sentence.
wordLabActivities.incorrectTitle: Look for the action and the time word

sentence.title: Lab Challenge A
sentence.rawText: Yesterday, our eco-club planted neem saplings.

wordLabActivities.correctFeedback: Spot on! 'Yesterday' is the past time clue, and 'planted' is the matching Past Simple verb.
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Select exactly two words: the time word at the start ('Yesterday') and the finite verb ('planted').
wordLabActivities.hint: Ask: Which word tells WHEN it happened, and which word is the action verb?

wordLabActivities.title: B. Sort Cards Into Past, Present & Future
wordLabActivities.instruction: Tap each logbook phrase, then tap Past, Present, or Future to place it.
wordLabActivities.promptText: 1. Tap a sentence card below, then tap Past, Present, or Future:

items.explanation: 'planted' and 'yesterday' place it in finished Past time.

items.text: is reading a science journal now
items.explanation: 'is reading ... now' is Present Progressive (ongoing now).
'will visit ... next month' points to Future time.
'rises ... daily' expresses a timeless Present truth.

items.text: are going to clean the garden tomorrow
items.explanation: 'are going to ... tomorrow' expresses a Future plan.

wordLabActivities.completeFeedback: Every slip is sorted onto the right point of the school timeline!
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Check the verb form ('planted/wrote' = Past; 'rises/is reading' = Present; 'will/going to' = Future). Tap any marked card to move it.

wordLabActivities.title: C. Rebuild a Present Perfect Record
wordLabActivities.instruction: Arrange the tiles in order to show an action completed earlier with a present result.
wordLabActivities.predicateText: have arranged the library books neatly.
wordLabActivities.correctFeedback: Excellent! Plural 'The students' pairs with 'have arranged', showing the shelves are tidy right now.
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Start with the Subject ('The students'), then the auxiliary ('have'), then the past participle ('arranged'), followed by the object.

wordLabActivities.title: D. Swap the Verb to Shift Time
wordLabActivities.instruction: Tap at least two verb forms to see how changing the verb shifts the sentence across time.

options.meaningEffect: Shows a regular healthy habit (Present Simple).
Shifts the event into finished Past time (Past Simple V2).
Moves the action into Future time.

wordLabActivities.takeaway: One verb slot controls whether the exact same healthy action sits in the Present, Past, or Future!

wordLabActivities.title: E. Complete the Timetable Notice
wordLabActivities.instruction: Pick the verb form that matches this scheduled school timetable notice for tomorrow.
wordLabActivities.sentenceAfterBlank: from the school gate at 7:00 a.m. tomorrow.

options.feedback: 'leaving' alone has no finite helper ('is leaving') and cannot complete the Predicate.
Correct! Official schedules and timetables for future events naturally use Present Simple ('leaves').
'left' refers to the past, which clashes with 'tomorrow'.

wordLabActivities.title: F. Fix the Stative Verb Slip
wordLabActivities.instruction: Read this flawed logbook note and diagnose what is wrong.
wordLabActivities.brokenSentence: Our school garden is belonging to every student in our school.
wordLabActivities.repairedSentence: Our school garden belongs to every student in our school.
wordLabActivities.question: Why does 'is belonging' need to be repaired?

options.label: 'belong' is a stative verb showing ownership, so it stays in Simple form ('belongs').
options.feedback: Exact diagnosis! State verbs like belong, know, own, and understand avoid '-ing'.

options.label: It should be 'are belonging' because there are many students.
options.feedback: Careful: the Subject is singular 'Our school garden', and 'belong' should not take '-ing'.

options.label: Nothing is wrong; every verb can take '-ing' in the present.
options.feedback: Not every verb—stative/non-conclusive verbs stay in Simple form.

independentPractice.cueText: First tap the time clue word in the sentence, then pick the matching verb form.
independentPractice.title: Challenge 1: Spot the Time Clue & Choose the Verb
independentPractice.instruction: Tap the word that tells us WHEN this action takes place, then repair the blank.
independentPractice.targetPrompt: Step 1: Tap the time-clue word in the sentence
independentPractice.imperativeQuestion: Step 2: Which verb completes 'Meera _____ fresh oranges yesterday.'?

imperativeOptions.label: buys
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'buys' is Present Simple, which clashes with 'yesterday'.

imperativeOptions.label: bought
imperativeOptions.feedback: Well done! 'yesterday' signals finished past time, so Past Simple 'bought' fits.

imperativeOptions.label: has bought
imperativeOptions.feedback: Do not pair Present Perfect ('has bought') with a finished past marker like 'yesterday'.

independentPractice.successFeedback: Great! 'yesterday' locks the sentence to Past Simple ('bought').
independentPractice.retrySubjectFeedback: Tap the single word at the end that tells us which day this happened.

independentPractice.cueText: Think about whether this is an ongoing moment or a repeated habit.
independentPractice.title: Challenge 2: Habit vs Happening Now
independentPractice.instruction: Choose the accurate verb form for this sentence.

sentence.title: Independent Check 2
sentence.rawText: Listen! The school choir _____ the morning prayer right now.

structureSummary.predicateText: is singing the morning prayer right now

independentPractice.imperativeQuestion: Which verb fits 'Listen! The school choir _____ the morning prayer right now.'?

imperativeOptions.label: sings
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'sings' expresses a daily habit, but 'Listen!' and 'right now' point to what is happening at this instant.

imperativeOptions.label: is singing
imperativeOptions.feedback: Correct! 'Listen!' and 'right now' signal Present Progressive ('is singing').

imperativeOptions.label: sang
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'sang' is Past Simple, whereas 'right now' is happening in the present.

independentPractice.successFeedback: Present Progressive captures actions in progress right now.

independentPractice.title: Challenge 3: Unfamiliar Sentence Diagnosis
independentPractice.instruction: Spot the correct sentence without any hints.

sentence.title: Independent Check 3
sentence.rawText: Which logbook entry is grammatically accurate?

imperativeOptions.label: Kabir is knowing how to play tabla since 2021.
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'know' is a stative verb (avoid 'is knowing'), and 'since 2021' links past to present.

imperativeOptions.label: Kabir has lived in Cuttack since 2021.
imperativeOptions.feedback: Exact! An action/state starting in 2021 and continuing up to now uses Present Perfect ('has lived ... since 2021').

imperativeOptions.label: Kabir will visited Konark next Sunday.
imperativeOptions.feedback: Never put a past form after 'will'—always use the base verb ('will visit').

independentPractice.successFeedback: You diagnosed stative verbs, future modals, and 'since' accurately on your own!

completionSummary.headline: Timeline Repaired! Lesson Complete!
completionSummary.celebrationMessage: Mira, Arjun, and Gyan placed every school logbook entry onto its true Past, Present, or Future spot.
learnedPoints: Time (Past, Present, Future) is when an event happens; Tense is the verb form used to express it.
Present Simple fits daily habits, facts, timetables, and stative verbs ('knows', 'belongs'); Present Progressive ('is writing') fits actions happening now.
Past Simple fits finished past markers ('yesterday'); Present Perfect ('has cleaned') connects earlier work to now; Future time uses 'will + base verb' or 'going to'.
repairedMessages: Yesterday, our eco-club planted neem saplings.
Mira is writing the science report now.
Our class will visit the planetarium tomorrow.
